questions.question: What is the chemical structure of a triglyceride?
options: Glycerol + 2 fatty acids + a phosphate head
questions.explanation: A triglyceride is 1 glycerol backbone + 3 fatty acids — the main storage and dietary form of fat.

questions.question: Why is a saturated fatty acid solid at room temperature?
options: It has many double bonds that kink the chain
It has no double bonds, so its straight chains pack tightly
It is built from fused carbon rings
questions.explanation: Saturated = no double bonds → straight chains pack tightly → solid (butter, lard). Unsaturated fats have kinks → liquid (oils).

questions.question: What distinguishes a monounsaturated from a polyunsaturated fatty acid?
options: Mono has no double bonds; poly has one
Mono has one double bond; poly has two or more
Mono is always solid; poly is always liquid
Mono comes from animals; poly from plants
questions.explanation: Mono = 1 double bond; Poly = 2 or more double bonds.

questions.question: According to the exam tip, more double bonds in a fat means it is...
options: More liquid and more prone to spoilage
questions.explanation: ★ Exam tip: More double bonds = more liquid AND more prone to spoilage. Saturation drives whether a fat is solid or liquid.

questions.question: A phospholipid such as lecithin acts in food as a(n)...
questions.explanation: Phospholipids are amphipathic (water-loving head, fat-loving tails), so they build cell membranes and act as emulsifiers (e.g., lecithin).

questions.question: Which statements are true of phospholipids? (Select all that apply)
options: Made of glycerol + 2 fatty acids + a phosphate head
Amphipathic — water-loving head and fat-loving tails
Composed of four fused carbon rings
The body's main storage form of fat
questions.explanation: Phospholipids = glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate head, are amphipathic, and form cell membranes. Four fused rings describe sterols; the storage form of fat is triglycerides.

questions.question: Cholesterol is a sterol the body uses to make...
questions.explanation: Cholesterol (four fused carbon rings) is the main sterol — used to make hormones, vitamin D, and bile.

questions.question: Which two fatty acids are essential (the body cannot make them)?
questions.explanation: Linoleic and linolenic are the two essential fatty acids — the body can't make them, so they must come from food.

questions.question: Saturated fats are mostly from animals. Which two PLANT oils are the exceptions (high in saturated fat)?
questions.explanation: ★ Exam tip: Saturated = solid + mostly animal; the two plant exceptions are palm and coconut oil.

questions.question: Where does most fat digestion occur, and what emulsifies the fat there?
options: Small intestine; bile (made in liver, stored in gallbladder)
questions.explanation: The small intestine is the main site. Bile (made in the liver, stored in the gallbladder) emulsifies fat; pancreatic lipase then breaks triglycerides into fatty acids + monoglycerides.

questions.question: After absorption into intestinal cells, dietary fat is repackaged into chylomicrons and travels through the ___ before entering the blood.
questions.explanation: Fat digestion products enter intestinal cells, are repackaged into chylomicrons, and travel through the lymph before entering the blood.

questions.question: As particles go chylomicron → VLDL → LDL → HDL, they become...
questions.explanation: ★ Exam tip: chylomicron → VLDL → LDL → HDL, particles get denser (less fat, more protein). Remember HDL = Healthy = to the liver.

questions.question: Which vitamins does dietary fat carry and help absorb?
questions.explanation: Fat carries and absorbs the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

questions.question: What is the AMDR (acceptable range) for total calories from fat?
questions.explanation: The Food & Nutrition Board's AMDR for fat is 20–35% of total calories.

questions.question: What best describes atherosclerosis?
options: A sudden drop in blood cholesterol
Plaque (cholesterol, fat, inflammation) builds up inside artery walls, narrowing them
A deficiency of essential fatty acids
questions.explanation: Atherosclerosis is plaque buildup (cholesterol, fat, inflammation) inside artery walls → arteries narrow and stiffen → can block blood flow → heart attack or stroke.

flashcards.back: 1 glycerol backbone + 3 fatty acids — the main storage and dietary form of fat.
Having both a water-loving (hydrophilic) head and fat-loving (hydrophobic) tails — describes phospholipids.
Lipoprotein that carries absorbed dietary fat from intestinal cells through the lymph into the blood.
"Healthy" lipoprotein; densest (most protein, least fat), carries cholesterol back to the liver.

questions.question: Which element makes protein unique compared with carbohydrates and fats?
questions.explanation: Protein contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and — uniquely — nitrogen. Nitrogen sets protein apart from carbs and fat.

questions.question: How many amino acids are there in total, and how many are essential?
questions.explanation: There are 20 amino acids total; 9 are essential (must come from food).

questions.question: Why must ALL essential amino acids be present to build a given protein?
options: Protein synthesis is all-or-nothing — if one runs low (the limiting amino acid), that protein can't be built
Each amino acid builds a separate organ
The body stores extra amino acids for later use
Non-essential amino acids cannot be made by the body
questions.explanation: Protein synthesis is all-or-nothing. If even one essential amino acid runs low (the 'limiting' amino acid), the body can't build that protein.

questions.question: A peptide bond forms through a condensation reaction when...
options: Two fatty acids attach to a glycerol
The amino group of one amino acid links to the acid group of the next
questions.explanation: A peptide bond forms when the amino group of one amino acid links to the acid group of the next (a condensation reaction).

questions.question: What is denaturation of a protein?
options: Building a protein from amino acids
Heat, acid, or agitation unravels the protein's shape, so it loses function (usually permanent)
Absorbing amino acids into the blood
questions.explanation: Denaturation: heat, acid, or agitation unravels the shape → the protein loses function (e.g., cooking an egg, stomach acid). The unfolding is generally permanent.

questions.question: What ultimately determines a protein's function?
options: The order of amino acids, which sets its folded 3-D shape
The number of peptide bonds only
Whether it is animal- or plant-based
questions.explanation: Sequence → shape → function: the order of amino acids makes the chain fold into a specific 3-D shape, and that shape determines what the protein does.

questions.question: Which foods are HIGH-quality (complete) proteins containing all essential amino acids? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Complete proteins are animal foods (meat, fish, eggs, dairy) plus soy. Legumes are moderate quality; grains and vegetables are low quality (incomplete).

questions.question: Legumes (beans, lentils, peanuts) are considered what quality of protein?
questions.explanation: Legumes (beans, lentils, peanuts) are moderate-quality protein.

questions.question: What are complementary proteins?
options: Combining two incomplete plant proteins so their limiting amino acids cover each other
Proteins that denature at the same temperature
questions.explanation: Complementary proteins combine two incomplete plant proteins so their limiting amino acids cover each other (e.g., rice + beans, peanut butter + bread).

questions.question: Which nutrient is the classic 'vegan gap' because it occurs naturally in animal foods only?
questions.explanation: ★ Exam tip: B12 is the classic vegan gap — it's naturally found in animal foods only.

questions.question: In the stomach, what starts breaking protein into shorter chains?
options: The enzyme pepsin (with hydrochloric acid denaturing the protein first)
questions.explanation: In the stomach, hydrochloric acid denatures protein and the enzyme pepsin starts breaking it into shorter chains.

questions.question: Where is protein finally broken into individual amino acids, and by what?
options: Small intestine; pancreatic and intestinal proteases
questions.explanation: In the small intestine, pancreatic and intestinal proteases finish the job, breaking chains into individual amino acids, which are absorbed into the blood and sent to the liver.

questions.question: Which are functions of protein in the body? (Select all that apply)
options: Build and repair tissue (its top priority)
Serve as the body's FIRST choice for energy
questions.explanation: Protein builds/repairs tissue, makes enzymes/hormones/antibodies, maintains fluid & pH balance, and transports substances. It provides energy only as a LAST resort — not the first choice.

questions.question: A person in POSITIVE nitrogen balance is...
options: A healthy, stable adult at equilibrium
questions.explanation: Positive = building tissue (growth, pregnancy, muscle gain). Equilibrium = healthy stable adult. Negative = losing tissue (illness, injury, starvation).

questions.question: What is the AMDR for calories from protein?
questions.explanation: The AMDR for protein is 10–35% of calories.

questions.question: What is the RDA for protein?
options: 0.8 g per kg of body weight
2.2 g per kg of body weight
0.8 g per lb of body weight
questions.explanation: The RDA is 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight.

questions.question: A 175-lb person's protein RDA is about 64 g/day. How is that calculated?
questions.explanation: Weight in lb ÷ 2.2 = kg, then × 0.8 = grams/day. 175 ÷ 2.2 = 79.5 kg × 0.8 ≈ 64 g.

questions.question: What happens to protein eaten beyond what the body needs?
options: It is stored as extra muscle protein
Nitrogen is removed (as urea) and the carbon skeleton is burned for energy or stored as fat
questions.explanation: ★ Exam tip: Extra protein isn't stored as protein — nitrogen is removed (as urea) and the carbon skeleton is burned for energy or stored as fat.

questions.question: Which best describes KWASHIORKOR?
options: Too little of BOTH calories and protein → severe wasting, 'skin and bones'
Enough calories but too little protein → swelling/edema and fatty liver
Excess protein intake straining the kidneys
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor = enough calories but too little protein → swelling/edema (belly) and fatty liver, often when a child switches to a starchy diet.

questions.question: Which condition results from too little of BOTH calories and protein?
questions.explanation: Marasmus results from too little of both calories and protein → severe wasting, 'skin and bones,' stunted growth.

flashcards.back: The essential amino acid in shortest supply; it caps how much of a protein the body can build.
Unraveling of a protein's 3-D shape by heat, acid, or agitation, causing loss of function (usually permanent).
Two incomplete plant proteins combined so their limiting amino acids cover each other (e.g., rice + beans).
Enough calories but too little protein → edema (swollen belly) and fatty liver.
Too little of BOTH calories and protein → severe wasting, 'skin and bones.'

questions.question: Which of these RAISES basal metabolic rate (BMR)?
options: More lean muscle mass, fever, or stimulants like caffeine
questions.explanation: BMR is raised by more lean muscle mass, growth, fever, stress, stimulants (caffeine/nicotine), cold exposure, and a taller/larger body.

questions.question: Which factors RAISE BMR? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Raise BMR: more lean muscle, growth, fever, stress, stimulants, cold exposure, larger body. Aging and low-calorie dieting LOWER BMR.

questions.question: Which of these LOWERS BMR?
options: Aging, muscle loss, and low-calorie dieting
questions.explanation: BMR is lowered by aging, loss of muscle, and low-calorie dieting/fasting (the body conserves energy).

questions.question: Where does digestion fit into energy expenditure?
options: It is the largest part of basal metabolism
It is NOT part of basal metabolism — it's the separate thermic effect of food
It is counted the same as physical activity
questions.explanation: ★ Exam tip: Digestion is NOT part of basal metabolism — it's the separate thermic effect of food.

questions.question: What is the METRIC formula for BMI?
questions.explanation: Metric BMI = kg ÷ m². (Imperial: lb ÷ in² × 703.)

questions.question: What is the IMPERIAL (US) formula for BMI?
questions.explanation: Imperial BMI = lb ÷ in² × 703. Metric = kg ÷ m².

questions.question: What is a key limitation of BMI?
options: It doesn't directly measure body fat — muscular people can read as 'overweight,' and it ignores where fat sits
questions.explanation: BMI doesn't directly measure body fat — muscular people can read as 'overweight,' and it ignores where fat is distributed.

questions.question: Upper-body / central ('apple-shaped') fat distribution is associated with...
options: Visceral fat around the abdomen and higher risk of heart disease and diabetes
Fat stored mainly on the hips and thighs
questions.explanation: Upper-body/central ('apple') = visceral fat around the abdomen → higher risk of heart disease and diabetes.

questions.question: Lower-body ('pear-shaped') fat on the hips and thighs is associated with...
options: Higher risk of heart disease and diabetes
questions.explanation: Lower-body ('pear') = fat on hips/thighs → lower disease risk than central/visceral fat.

questions.question: Waist-circumference 'red flags' signaling higher risk are greater than...
questions.explanation: Waist circumference red flags: greater than 40 inches (men) or 35 inches (women) signals higher risk.

questions.question: What is a healthy, sustainable rate of weight loss?
questions.explanation: Aim for slow, steady loss — about 1–2 lb per week.

questions.question: Why do fad diets (like a cereal 'kick start') typically fail long-term?
options: Weight drops short-term, but returns once old habits resume because the change wasn't sustainable
questions.explanation: ★ Exam tip: Fad diets cut calories short-term so weight drops — but it returns once old habits resume because the change wasn't sustainable. Focus on sustainable lifestyle change.

questions.question: Which are healthy weight-management strategies? (Select all that apply)
options: Aim for 1–2 lb loss per week
Control portions and choose whole/nutrient-dense foods
Rely on fad/crash diets for fast results
questions.explanation: Healthy strategies: slow steady loss (1–2 lb/wk), portion control, whole foods, watching liquid calories, and staying active. Fad/crash diets aren't sustainable.

flashcards.back: Calories the body burns at rest to stay alive. Raised by muscle, fever, stimulants; lowered by aging and dieting.
Energy used to digest food — separate from basal metabolism (digestion is NOT part of BMR).
Apple = central/visceral abdominal fat (higher heart-disease & diabetes risk); pear = hip/thigh fat (lower risk).
Fat stored around abdominal organs; linked to higher risk of heart disease and diabetes.
